Definition: Credit-claiming is when a senator claims personal (or shared) responsibility for a desirable government action or outcome—typically particularized benefits delivered to their state (federal grants, appropriations, projects, disaster designations, military missions, appointments), legislative accomplishments (bills passed, amendments adopted, provisions included in advancing legislation), or successful influence over executive agency decisions.

Press releases announcing benefits to the state count even when the senator's role is implied by the act of announcing.

Negative clarification: Not credit-claiming: mere introduction/cosponsorship of legislation without advancement; explanations of votes or positions; criticism of opponents or administrations; advocacy letters/requests where no outcome has yet been achieved; ceremonial items (honoring others, condolences, commemorations, contests); statements supporting nominees or welcoming decisions the senator did not claim to influence; oversight questioning without claimed results; general partisan cheerleading.
